EXTRAORDINARY SCENR AT AN ACCTION.—A sale had been advertised to take place on Monday afternon at a tavern in Crewe, but on the auctioneer presenting itinielf at the house a little before the sale wasannounced to commence he lan d both shop and private door barrol against him. Pre- cautions had been token to place a hailer in possession, but somehow or other he had been got out, and the auctioneer could now find no means of obtaining an entrance. In vain he knocked and shouted at the window. and he was obliged to resort to force. A crowbar WAR speedily procured, and the window was unfastened, but no sooner did the auctioneer', bead appear at the into =pace than a woman inside hit him a blow on the hood. The woman', efforts were backed up by a man and a younger female inside, both of whom Wendy declared he shou'd Oct come in. Finding he could not obtain access through the window, the auctioneer turned to the door, and no sooner was the door open than a fearful battle" took place. One of the females was„ with considerable difficulty, restrained from using a pair of longs on the auctioneer's face, two men, however. interfered, though not until she lied succeeded in giving hint a black eye. The others set upon him, and scratched his face, and so maltreated him that he appeared glad to bick not into the street. The door was then slammed in his rice. and the inmates grinned at him through the window. he anaistance of the police was invoked, but the sale was ' not held. The auctioneer's aesistauts were severely handled.

SATURDAY, JUNE 12. 1880.

Tau Government Hares and Rabbits Bill was by the Some Secretary submitted for • second reading to the House df Camino., on Thursday evening, but owing to the night being nearly wholly taken up with Mr. explantion of his financial pro- posals, and the discoseion thereon, the debate on the Bill was adjourned. The Bill h. met with opp.ition from sporting gentlemen on both Bidee of the House. It is one of the measures that the Premier, when a candidate for Midlothian, led age lc/Atari/its to believe would be introduced when • Liberal Government came into power ; and tenant farmers, who have long stvod in need of protection against the ravage. of ground game, which sporting landowners have insisted upon being maintained upon the crops of their tenantry, welcomed the promi.d protection with open arms, sod no doubt, a. a ...fluent., in many parts they made their influence felt in the ballot box at the late elections. The opponents of the bill condemn it from various etand points, and we should be glad if we were able to say that selfiahnese is not the ham of opposition. The opponents object to the tenant farmer having the right to kill, or to preserve upon hia holding, game that will devour hie crops, and one : sect of the opp.itionists is in fear that /porting will be put an end to, and that country districts will realioo the worst apprehensions of Colonel John Ireland Blackburide, who thinks that no greeter .lamity could betel a neighbourhood that to lose its landed , gentry. This sect contends that the preservation or destruction of ground game should boa matter of contract between the land ownerand tenant, but, after the experience of contracts between landlords and tenants in the cute of the Agricultural Holdings Act, not only tenant farmers, but those unconnected with agricultural .arcely need persuading that ' such freedom of contract invariably ends in the strong obtaining all they seek, and the weak being driven by neoesmty to concede everything .ked, and finally going to the wall. Other opponents argue:that if the farmer is given control over the ground game he may suffer bar. and rabbi. to multiply to a degree that they will become 11111Der0118 enough, not only to devour the produeo of a farmer's own fields, but to invade the grounds of hie neighbour and play havock with the crops of the latter, though he may be anxious to limit the Fame on hie holding. Soar of these contentions will bear Close scrutiny in the face of the fact that a farmer who toils and spends his capital upon his farm to produce crops ought to be empowered to protect his crops from destruction, or if he prefers to have them eaten up to have control over that which he is willing shall devour the prodoie of hie fields, just as in the case of Ids cattle. The dillecent sections of opponents to the Bill hold, thereidre, on the one hand that ground game will be annihilated and eporting put an end to, and on the other hand maintain that farmers will permit ground game to become more numerous than ever. At present the farmer is powerleee against the wish of the c.aee of the soil, if the latter initiate upon game being preserved, and the Bill of the Government seeks to confer upon the farmer the protection that he now sadly feels the want of. By the Bill the land- lord will not be debarred from shooting ground game on his tenant's holding, but will be at liberty to shoot

concurrently with hi. tenant, to that the right ill] the game is not transferred wholly front the landlord at the tenant. By the Bill it la &imply propoeed that n• oontrart between a landlord and tenant for the latter to preeerve the game for the sod. 11110 and pleaattre of the former shall hire a binding eff.rt, but that tb• tenant than hare, what he bar not hi•herto had, el, cept through the generosity of his landowner, 'be lciral right, either by himself or his agents, to th... 4 hares and rabbits in hi- field., and thus to protect the crop§ by which he NMut hie livelihood from being devoured.

The House of lt melons had a most important topic introduced for its musiderat ion •,n Monday lam, and though it elicited nu very protnicted diseuesion, net a vital pnamise was evoked that will render the day memorable in the annals if the House, as ha ing the date on which a aerie. blow was dealt at the practice ot flogging in the navy eerviee. Elebtees in every borough will remember the excited politics/ haranguee that were delivered on the rye of the last election, the majority of which were made to bear ea this jaeotion; and mural literature, aided by pictorial are, vividly conveyed to hurgesam the necessity of abrogating n puniahment which received the invari- able appellation of •• brutal and degrading." The majority of gentlemen Imbued with Liberal opinion., who appealed to constitueneies. were prolific with yromisse for the antithilation of retch a rude and barber°. system td ras•igetion ; and now it A a satisfaetion to announee that the hue act in a drama whirh was supported and applauded by the late Government is about to be hissol off the stage and ronsigued to that oblivion it hue merited so Political tournaments haveolten been waged, in which chanthionia for and against the extinei ion of this mode oa Milo:Bon in the maritime emelt* home displayed unlimited valour, but ma one ever advocated its total abolition Mon' Leblininly mid ardently than the hon. member for Leiemter, und the el. 41111,1 t who now to ably .ss•upicei the pmit not of Chanoellor of the Duth/ of Laneuscer 1,, 1,7, Mr. Peter Taylor brought forward emotion for the abolition of floggoig in the nary, and in 1879 tho ynci.tioit again rose upon the Army Dieeipline Bill in regard to the floggin • of marines, at which tune Lead lintiffirton mov:ff • reemlution to the effect that no bill would be sataafae- tory which provided for the permanent retention of corporal punishment for military offences. Subse- quently toe right bon. member for Birmingham, whom support for any humanitarian questim is always consiatently given, aueneeded, niter the most lAMB°. effort, in eouvineing.• stubborn Opposition of the ' righteousnese of hie came, and managed to effect • ! reduction of the hundred crime for which onetiga. ' Bon ty the •• cat " was invariably beetowed to one- tontli ; and but for the violent moist...nee of the then Miniaterialiste ita total annulment would have ' been aisompliehed, and the inhuman treat. fluent to which our brave men are today subjected would have been a thing of the past. Mr. Oond, who introduced the subject on Monday evening, excited Opposition cheers his vivid description of the way «leonine are mane at Bumingham, quAing several remarks made ir7r Mr. Chamberlain pertinent to the question, and alludiug derisively ton plaeard containing a Molar. of a naked ...Idler being flogged for his offences, the letterprem underneath the picture Mime characterised be the %neither as of n •• minute amel disgusting dmeription." He believed the stiff ratites of the Be- lmingbam eleetors were expressly invited on the ground that it was the Tory party no opposed to the Liberals who maintain,' flogginz in the %Any and navy. Mr. Gomm then, in an excellent peroration. demanded that shim a lalge number of flee Majesty'a Onvernmen t en the I Ministerial ode—had obtained offiem by promisee Ito ebtlish that system tif treatment hi the naval ! and military Perrin..., whether they were Apared ' fiunlly and pm...al-Luny to 'abolish that kind of punishment. NOne were more pleawed than Mr. Taylor, Mr. Bright, and when, who have !slotted no diligently to bring shout a reformation in thin system, when the Secretary to the Admiralty ram and in a apeech which elicited the warmed cheer., stated them the Board of Admiralty bad coucluded to premien an amendment to the Naval Dimipliue Act, whieh would omit flogging from the authorised puniehwents thereon enacted. Queetions then arise . to the aubetitutionary uneseures to be adopted since it:diction is deemed no neemenry to ensure preper discipline, bat nothing bin, evoked from the Secretary to the Admiralty, Mr. Childem rose and explained that he had made enquirim into the question of pub- oitune, and he had no doubt lint that next sebnion the Governmeut would modal, a meseure I which would be thoretughly aatisfact cry to them who had supported the abolition el il,gging in the army. It is a matter of extreme congratulatent . that a punitive measure which hee Men upheld to long to the disgrace of Englith legialatien is about to be abolish, el, and though nautical fire- eaters may bemoan that the •• service is going to doge," yet it is tettafmtory to know that discipline . can be obtained without im breach being visited . with an infliction that degradee the receiver in. stead of awakening him to the Moral principle. The Cameroniane hove been described an fanatics and an intolerant sent, but pee- emotion hats always been the mother of fanaticism, and has driven men to adopt extreme means to wurare and preserve human liberty. The Cameroniatte were inflamed with a paseion for liberty and prompted try the encroachments of Kingly eupremacy to guard it. It would be idle to attempt to defend all that the Covenantern did or supported, but they were undoubt- edly the forerunnern of the Revolution. Tlmugh the opinions proodtimed by Cameron in the Market . plarp of Rinquhar on the 20th June, 1680, were held by statesmen to be extnsme, impracticable, revolutionary, and utterly beneath attention, his indictment and repudiatien of the Monarchy were to all intents and purposes embodied in the Bill of Rights in the follow• ins year. The Cameronians still preserve their existence es a distinct religious body both in the old country, in America, and the Colonies, and they have always bees to the fore in the advocacy of human freedom. We doubt not they will celebrate the martyrdom of their founder with becoming piety and seal.

Annotvn EXTILOnDINSItY Otrrnao• no WARRINGTON. —On Thursday afternoon, an outrage and readier, of an extraordinary nature was perpetrated in Raydock.street. Warrington. About three o'clock, a Scotch packman named William Murray, was proceeding down the above street, when the door of a house was suddenly opened, and two men emerged therefrom, seized the panto., dragged him into the house, and locked the door. Before he could recover from the ourprise, a bandage was passed over his eyes and socurely tied, hie mouth piggish awl his lee and arms ACCUMI With • chain. The men in the house, whose soleoldect ams.ared to be that of plunder, then took hold of the pack and rifled ita contents, Inking a girl's black diagonal cloth jacket, value 10s., a woman's Rob Roy wool shawl, value 10s.; one 'cartel shoulder shawl, value:fs. tkl., two other Shetland stockings, value 30. BJ.; two yards brown Holland, value Is. 4d.; mid two yards ruse-coloured lama, va!ue 3s. Bd. The thieves also took from the person of the packman a ailver hunter watch of a Chinese pattern, widen amalgam guard, valuel3s. One of the assailants is described by the packman as being , • short stiff Irishman, wearing a black cord fmir of trousers, I and the other man is stated to have been a big, tall fellow. I 'The unfortunate hawker, otter retnaining with his eyes bandaged for 8i hours was then turned out of the house, when he male the biot of Ins way to the police station. The polka, although aceptimil of the man's statement, at once investigated the matter, and discovered that the tale wall mire invention. The pack of which he stated he had been robbed was found in .1111M1 .1' 3 AIM which he indicated. about three,oarters of a mile along Mancliester.road, by Inspector Singleton. The pawnbrokers in town were ap- prised of the alloi,ed robbery of the watch, when one of them informed the police that it had been pawned will, biro three days previously by the prisoner. The packruan, will probe- bly repent of booing related such an imaginative story to the police, cent are infortned he has been apprehended and will be brought before the magistrates this morning on a charge of vagrancy. and will have to account for setting the law io motion without junt Gaon, " . .

. . or Mn. J. P. REVNOLDS.—On Wednesday at St. James's Chinch, Birkdale, the marriage between Mr. John P. Reynolds and Miss Edith Crossley, of Birkdale, took j place. The cereinony was performed by the Rev. C. C. Reynolds. vicar of Wray, near Lancaster, and the Rev. G. • 1 F. Reynolds, late senior i",urate of Morcambe, brothers of the j bridegroom. The bide was given away by her uncle Mr. j John Crossley, of Briar's Hey, Rainhill. At the cmclusion , of the service.the Wedding March was played on the organ by Mr. Wm. Crossley, of Dolgelly. After the usual signing I of names in the vestry, the party returned to the residence of the bride's mother, and shortly afterwards the happY I 1 couple left for their honeymoon, which will be spent partly ill the lake district, and partly at Birchwood, Arnside, the country residence of Mr. John Cro,slev. which has been kindly placed at their disposal. He thonght they would all agree with the [ observations of the coroner. It was well known that bodies I were often found in the river, which bad to be taken to house. eituated in the midst of a dense population, and this could not but be prejudicid to Ho public health. It might be asked why the provision of such a building should not he left to the Commissioners, but he reminded the B.,ard that it war, in a sense, immaterial whether they pro- vided it or the Commit...loner., I,,,stlec in either case the money would have to come out of the pockets of the ratepayer.. a i,osirtlon to en:el the buildingtnost economically, because they hod the nocemary land upon which to put it. Such. structure might, for instance, be put up where their official FONCiI shed now was. Of course, if the Commissioners undertook to do the work.they would be at a great dis- advantage in having to purchase the ground in a suitable locality. He suppoeed the carrying out of each a ochertte would probably coat the Board something like £4O. The speaker then quoted front the 42ml section of the Burials Act, which stated that it should be lawful for any Burial Board, with the approval of the vestry, to provide it and proper placer in It fich bodies might In received and taken care of previously to interment, and to make arrangement. for the reception and care:of bodiee to be deposited therein, for such purpose they might exerciee the powers rested them by the Act for providing burial round.. When plans and tenders were uoknd for on the construction of the cemetery, two-thirds of those sent in showed a design for a mortuary, but the expense was considered tea great for the ratepayer. to enter into at the time. He moved that a vestry meeting should be oiled to obtain the opinion of the ratepayers as to whether they we.e agreeable to the Burial Board erecting a mortuary on land in the cemetery. The speaker also observed that it would be quite possible to hold the inqueets ill the cemetery oftice,and than the budies would Oct have to be carried through the town to often. Mr. !console eecontled the motion. Mr. COGZanini referred to the 143rd section of the Public Health Act, which reads an follows Any local authority may provide and maintain a proper place (otherwise than at a workhouse ore mortuary) for the reception of dead Ixalies during the time required to conduct any putt-wortent examination ordered by the coroner. or other constituted authority, and may make regulations with respect to the management of each place and where any such place has been provided, a coroner, or other constituted authority, may order the removal of the body to and from such phre, for carrying out each po,t morient examination. such cost of removal to be paid in the same manner and out of the same brat ae the costs and fees for port m.rtrad examinations when ordered by the coroner." Mr. Coleburn contended that according to that section they must not only have a mortuary, but a morn wherein puse taortene examination. could he held. They could lime a building adjoining the mortuary outside the cemetery, but the Local Government Board would not allow them to have a building for the hold- ing of such examinations inside the cemetery. The CHAIRMAN could not think that the section meant that they had not power to erect a rootu for the 1101.1114 el such examinations in the cemetery. Mr. Handley, Mr. Marshall, and Mr. Dobson took the sante view of the question as the chairman. After some further discussion, the motion of Mr. Marshall was passed unanimously.

A first N. 13 ritP,ON.—Two youths living at Fulwood, rivals for the affections of a cert;in young lady, also resi- dent there, quarrelled over the matter a few dive ago. and one of them challenged the other Co mortal combat with pistols. The meeting actually did take plue, one of the second. providing the firearms. in the ground. however. it , was proposed that the quarrel should be settled by fisticuffs, , and not by lethal weapons, but the more heroic of the two lovers rejected the proposal with scorn, and declared that only one of them should leave the spot alive. Whereupon the pistole were handed to them ; they were placed back to back, told to walk six paces each, and then turn round and fire. Them instructions were carried out, but it was impos- sible to tell at what 000 01 them was aiming the other tired over the head of his antagonist, the wad dropped on his fore- head, and he fell in • heap to the ground. ft wee soon Cooed, however. that fright alone was the cause of the fall. : While the seamde were endeavouring to ascertain the extent of It. injury • policeman was seen in the distance, and the whole party " stuttered " away behind the hedges The I pistol. were loaded in the preeence of the combstants, but ! the bullets were—blacklead.

A-NIUSE.AIi.NTS OF WARRINGTON.

Sir,—Sime weeks 000 letters appeared in your paper on the amoaements of Warriogton, complaining of the small number uf places of ri creation and amusement, he. There in no doubt tbat, consifif ring the population of Warrington, the places both of orm,ment and recreation are very There is Lo Wetmore.% Char.!, or Young Men's Institute, no gyfonasium.x trey poor thf airy, and nothing infthe shape of loftlly gad." MI e}4,1.111,“ the park, which is cerMinly pleasant enough, tut in most large towns each park is pro- vided with a recreation ground, fitted with horizontal bars, nings neolting horses, [MM., Sc. Then again, the railway oompanies do not furnish Saturday afternoon excursions as frequently as they might do. From Liverpool they may go to Ilancfiester and hack for half-a-crown, and from filen- °nester to Liverpool and back for the mme price. In some towns they have what are termed "Saturday Evenings for die People Schoolrooms are often used forth, purpose where the people may listen to readings, recitations, glee, song, . and • very enjoyable evening spent at a very low obarge. as the performers (mostly amateurs/ give their ser- vices grille. Wlfy might not emnething of the kind be at- tempted lit Warrington ? Surely there one sufficient people here to warmot such a trial being made. We have two political clubs, but of one, the Conservative,l know nothing, but the Liberal Club ,toes not appear to have mu.ll to re- commend it to the favourable notice of the thinking portion of our young men. Card.playing, billiard, and newspaper. cent! all theft, required for making good politicians, and unfortunately the two first sem to be the principal attrac- tion. No doubt if pays." hut does it instruct? Liberal Lfiuto ought to be something more than electioneering filth.o. If an addition erre, made to the number of books in Ike reading room and a library formed, with books on bin- tore. political economy, essays on political subject, dm., much good might be done. In the winter seasons, too, lee- r..., or reeding, might be given, and essays read : ore politreal debating society might be formed, fitting young men to take part in the prom., of the future. A good knowledge of the past and present ltiatory of our country sad its dopendencies, with a knowledge of the forms of government of other nations, and the great reforms and danger that have taken place in England and abroad, would bent good service to young men. Sir—Your report of the leg Prenot Guardian erecting gives the public a glimpse orate workhouse management, and It would seem the Guardians are becoming afire toevils which, I should think, they ought to have chuked long ago. For some time tradesmen have been unable to get their claims against the Union paid when due, anal have been told in excuse that the Elnan, Committee had not met, or that there was no money in the hank to the credit of the (hur- dle, the rate-collectors not having paid in the calls upon their townships. Neither of these hindrances need occur if there is any desire for the contrary. Why are not finance meetings called to pass tradesmen'e accounts at the close of each quarter? And why is it not found out that there is me money before it ie actually wanted? If the calls were ordered to be paid in say • month before the quarter end, or two months if need be, then there would he time for premurc to he put on the right parties, and the credit of the Union would he mvul. A miscalculation may arise with the beet, but for these to occur so frequently it must be that the Union business is condor.' in a very loose way by some one. I never heard it comp!ained of in the late clerk's time that accounts were not promptly meter that threats had to be used to secure payment. A Guanlian lately referred to tile matter, and was pertly answered, "The world wasn't made in a day anti on another occasion, to bolster up olficial indolence. it we, retorted, "Groat bodies tnove slowly." Let the Guardians be firm, and have their business attendwl lose buainess nen have a right to expect, and not take such evasive sowers from slow or fast officials, and then complainte on the part of ratepayers would occur lees freouently.—Yours respectfully, A RATEPAYER. I'. HAINES, Minister, jute 7th, 1880, Trinity M Frodsham. - - ST. lIELENs SE RAGE SCIIFME A joint meeting of the 'Health and raving Committees, was held on Friday afternoon, the Mayor presiding. There were also present Aldermen Harrison, Councillors Twyford, Belcher, McKechnie, Mcßryde, Bishop, Riley, and Allen. The Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Craik) read part of Mr. Hart's report relative to the sewage scheme, of which the subjoined is an extract The present outlet for the whole sewage of St. Helens is the Sankey Brook it being con- veyed into that stream by doers and Itaine whose outlets are upon Its sides. The Eccleston Brook is practically clear upon entering the borough tel the boundary near Denton's Green. Between that point and Westfield-street several sewers discharge into It. In summer Dine there it little anti often no water flowing down the course of the brook, it being all taken up by a feeder to the canal at Spray'. Bridge ; condquently the raw sewage from the outlets discharge into the brook without there being any means of diluting or fluphing the sewage from various outlets, the flow being very slow on account of the flatness of the sewers, and is further retarded by the unevenness of the inert surface of the open brook, and the large quantities of brick and rubbish thrown into the brook by children. The crude sewage in the summer months is solnetirues ate dead stem!, drying and fermenting in the sun, throwing off a etrong stench and being often green. From Westfield-street the brook flows to Kitt's Bridge, • diatance of about 300 yards, and at that place it receives the sewem of Liverpool-road and Greenbank, the enoat thickly populated portion of the borough. In 'rummer time, at this point, there is littleer nothing else but raw sewage flowing down the brook, the smell from which is very strong. After passing this point it receives two or three sewers, together with the drainage from slaughter- hnusen, chemical workg and waste heap in its course. It afterwards receive, the sewage of the l'eadey Crone dis- trict then it passe. through Mends. Gamble and Kartz's premises, and flows between 'arge deposits of alkali waste towards Net, receiving the Rainford or Batten brook into It. Thence it flews on out of the borough towards Newton and Eariestown and Warrington. Immediate attention shoeild be given to the ventilation of the mwers, which is at present defective. Main aewers should remove waste water from streets and houses to the most appropriate outlet, there lobe dealt with by some process whirl, shall render the newage harmless; the newer, being laid at such depths as will effectually drain all boom basement, And cellars, and Ibe free Bran any risk of the backing up of water, the. No house drain should ever he joined to a sewer direct, ea even form a continuo. flue by which gases may flow into the house. There most be a break in the drain, and menon of ventilation so as not to cause a noise.e. Discredit is brought on both wee. and sewer ventilation in newly. sewered towns where cesspool's exist, and these am yen. nected coo, to overflow, or are emptied into the sewers. The refuse is putrid, and the stench mod offensive. Thom who are ignorant of the cause of the nuisance blame the Aewers, and desire to block the ventilation. The true remedy in to abolish the cesspools a.s quickly an possible, Hushing the sewers regularly and abundantly. In all cases where a sewer is laid within 100 feet of any portion of It dwelling, the cesspool, Ac., should be filled up, and all draina connected with the main, as the borough surveyor may direct. Then comes the question, "How shall the sewage be dealt with when it is at the °offal' ? There are 'several modes in operation through the country for dealing with !sewage, such or precipitation by chemicals, the. irriga- tion over land, and filtration through land. After considering , the result of the evidence respecting all these syntems brought ' under the notice of the engineers of the Local Government Board, the manclusinns arrived at ace—That town sevrage can best and most chelply lea disposed of and purified by the process of laud irrigation for local agricultoral purposes. where local circumstancm are favourable. The land Irriga- tion is not practicable in all cases, and therefore other modes of dealing with aewage must he allowed. In a town properly sewered and drainal, well supplied with water on a constant advice, and wholly water closeted, the stooge will be in the richest state, and may le dealt with at the leant cost, and with the greatest safety to health, either by ehemicals or irrigation on land. The drawback—and the only one to irrigation over land—is the large area required, which Ahould be rot lem than one acre for each 200 inhabitants, beside, making a reasonable margin for the increase of the population. This would require about 300 acre% and An far as Mr. Hart has been able to ascertain. there is no reason why this system of irrigation should not be adopted, taking all the sewage down below the elouble-locks at Reolmte (towarde Newmn), and having a : sewage farm there for its treatment. The surveyor gave a list of some towns that are adopting POMP mean, for the re- , moved and treatment of the sewage. Fifteen towns were adopting sewage by irrigation. By land filtration, Kendal. ' By precipitation of sewage sludge in tanks. Birmingham. By treatment with chemicals. Coventm", Bolton. Leeds. anti Bradfona By pail svatern, Manchester. Halifax, and Roch- dale. At Burnley the sewage is disposed of into tanks, and it is there treated in some manner by a company, at • cat to the borough of about sine shilling per head of the porn- ' lotion per annum. Perhaps some arrangements could he made with this company, if considered dmirable. It is known cc Major General Scutt's process. Considering the import- ance of the questinu. Mr. Hart suggested that the report len referred to the Highway Committee, to be read and con. siderel and that the report be printed, and a copy supplied In each member of the Town Council. Heal,e recommended that a complete eel of oleos awl estimate, be prepared, and a scheme submitted, Mewing the linm of peonage,' maim to the poine of outlet that may prove, by levelling, to be the hest ami most advantageeng leaving the question of dispoaal over for gone little time, to enable an inspection Co be made before arriving :it any definim concluaion. At the awe, inquiries might be made as to the term. and conditions upon which land might be obtained, cod that the whore nobler, Mould be con.sidered by the loint Committees of Faeingand Health. After some diaconal., it was decided. on the ro- wel:ion of Mr. Allen, eecon fed by Mr. Riley. that the Surveyor prepare estimate. as to the prahable cod of cleansing and draightening the brook, and improving the cfSatcLcy Brook, from Boardm en's lane bridge to Snrav's bridge.

On Tueaday at the Itailway Inn, Whine, an inquest was held hy Mr. C. E. Driffiold, county coroner, on the hotly ef John Makiason, aged 40, of Warrington, a foreman carpenter, ander the London and North-le:stern Hallway Co, who died very enddenly on Saturday morning, immediately after having misted in the unloading a wagon lotted with tim- ber, OW the Widnes station. Deceased had some short time ago suffered severely from bronchitis, but had for eeveral weeks been in very fair health, and his sodden ‘leath at tirst, thought to be attributable to breathing gne, from one

David Orf7rd, -41,—Napier.street, Warrington, said he laboured for the London and North-western joiners. and OW Saturday morning four of them—two joiners and two labourers—came from Warrington by goods train, which also brought their thnber and material, to Widnes. They arrived at Widnes about half-past seven, anti unloaded the material on the high level line, betweenthe junction and the station. They had just finished unloading, when he saw that deceased was just tumbling out of the wagon, and heard him shout David, Ifavitl." lie caught him in his arms before he got to the ground. Deceased wan mill that he could not stand up, and he began vomiting blood in • stream, as if it had loon pumped. He struggled for about three seeonds, but did sot speak after uttering the word ,••Devid.” One of the men ran for Mr. Brown, amintant to Dr. McDonnell, out deceased only lived about th,ee minutes, and was dead when the nurgeon arrived Whilst vomiting deceased must have lost at least two quarts of blood. lie 'bent known, and worked, with deceased about four yearn, 'cent he appeared as healthy and strong a nisn as he had ever known. The monthly meeting was held on Monday, Mr. Lvon in the chair. There were also present Meters. Norman, flotsam. Williams, Steele, I'. Speakman, Handley, Collier, J. J. Speakman, McDougall, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secre- tary h Barker (surveyor), and Mouths (medical officer.) The Law Cr max read the following (copy) letter which Bed keen received : Waterworks Mee, Ilunc..rn, May 11, laBo.—Dear Sir,— Acedding to my letter to ydu of the tilt iS.C.! heonehtth• oommunication from the Commlssioners, addressed to rite, es le their having under emsiderstion the desirability of t ur. °sand, the rights and property ot the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks mot whether the direetors would he mewed to enter Into negotiations for the sale thereof to the Oommlasioners, heMre the directors of the Waterworks Co.. at their lowa hi, meeting held yea.erdev. I hare the lem,ur to iseldrit, the Runeorn Lnprovement Bommissioners that the direrh.rs think they baron, power to negotiate wilt Die Corn- tedsskmers at present . apt they vein bring the sot,. before the proprietors at the annual meeting In August. little Com- missioners desire it —I am, dear Mr, yours tern truly. W. Y. —M M. Brookes. Esq., secretary, Pohl. Oftiem. Runcorn. Str. SPeagnan proposed, and Mr. Maastram, seconded a motion referring the letter to the Highway and Sanitary Comtnittee. Mr. Cot tan I should have thought that they would would have teen glad to have got shut of the shares. Mr. NORMAN No, the shares are now beginning to pay. Mr. Cobble.: Whin is the interest Mr. Noumea Two and a half per rent. -Mr. Cottran I think that is very vague. If they have • mind h. bring it before the authorities belonging to the Waterworks Co., let them do so, and then inform us act. whether they are wield.] to dispose of the works. I do not at all see why we should be at their beck and cal;. [The Chairman We made the fret advance.] Certainly we made the first advance, but look at what is the nature of the reply. The proper course ia to let them he preparod, sad then let on know, when we can respond. I propose that the communication he laid upon the table, seeing that them 4 is nothing in it really to refer to any committee. Mr. Doseow : I eecond the motion. We hare already MlMl,Meanees to the Waterworks Company, and I think it is now their duty to communicate with us before we mai:* any further advawee. Mr. NORMAN The directors distinctly state that if it is the wish of the Commiseioners, they will bring the matter before ahareholdere la the meeting in August NI, COLLIN,: What does our letter cute? Does it not say tlmt it is the wish of the Commissioners? If, however, they are not prepared to take action, let the communication lie there (pointing to the table). I have no doubt in the least in my mini that they wish to get rid of the water. works. . .

.7h; amendment was put, on which four mesitime voted for it and four against it. The Clunawart I shall vote for the letter being laid be- fore the Highway and Sanitary Committee, because I think that, as we made the first advance, it in only courteous to Lin Waterworks Company that the letter should be fairly considered. The motion for the adoption of the minutes was then passed.

This document.,—;FLlr WL--t:r'es;;;;1-1..y Dr. Mmrits, stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the month of May was 23, representing a death rats 01 19 per 1.000 por annuli). Of these eight were due to dis- eases of the respiratory organs, five to diseases of the brain,. three to abdominal affections, two to senile decay. and two to marasmus. Disease of the heart, cancer, and typhoid fever accounted for one (loath each. Of the deaths, nine were those of children tier years and under, and of these nix were one year and under. One inquest was held, rocking the total deaths 24. Fifty births took place during the month, being a birth rate 01 42 per 1.000 per annuni.

About a quarter past one o'clock on Thursday morning a fire, which teas most diaastroua in its effects, was discovered to have broken out in the joiners' chop on the premises of Messrs. Collin and Son, builders, Academy-street, Warring- ton. The building, which were two storeys high, consisted of three joiners' and machine shop, and contained moon valuable machinery, comprising circular 8.11,1, planing and moulding machines, joiners' tools, Ac. Two of the building, Hood side by side in the middle of the yard, and were flanked by a drying Abed on the one aide, and by an engine and bniler house on the other. The third build- ing, which we, situated behind them, and abutted on Itigby- street, contained in the upper story about thirty joiners' benches and 3 quantity of finished joiners' work, the 1011, crony being occupied hy a number of machines. The build- ings were aurrounded ho a large quantity of deal and caber thaber cut up and in bulk. The fire was first seen boo man from the gasworks and a police officer, and they at once raised an Alarm. In a short time the new steam tire engine, the "Major,'' was on the arm, and two jets were brought into operation, a third hose being attached to the main in Academy-ntreet. When discovered the portion in donee woe the rear of a joiners' alma, abutting on Rigby-ntreet„ but by the time the engine raln, got to work, the fire had spread vrith great rapidity to the adjoining chop,. The fiances rose to a great height owing to the combustible nature of the buildings, and their surroundings, and the heat was most intense. It was then very evident that there was no prospect of any at the shops being saved, and the attention of Mr. "hurley, the superin- tendent of the tire brigade, who together with Mr. Turner, hi, deputy, neveml firemen and the Chief-constable (Mr. Hone.) Inspector Protltt, Sorgeant Johnson, Sergeant Spinks, and a few constables, was in attendance, was directed to the preventing of the further spread of the tire. Sergeant Johnmn, with thisobjectdirected the jet he wasin charge of to the drying shed and the slacks of timber in cloee proximity, and was imgrumental in saving the greater part of the shell and also moat of the wood. The firemen were ably d directe by Mr. Chorley, end the fire engine, which war in chart, of Inapector Profitt,did it work most efficiently and was highly spoken of. By three o'clock the whole of the shops were completely destroyed, together with their contents, bt.t the firemen continued to play on the ruin, for Slime hours after- wants. The damage done by the flee is estimated at 5.4,000 or ES,(100, which is covered by insurance, but Measrs. Collin will auntain great Irma through the destruction of the finished wood work which was stored in the buildings, and which was intended for several contracts that firm have in hand. The fire, of the origin of which nothing, known, will he the means of throwing about 120 men out of em- ployment.

WINSPOIIO AND SOLO Winsford and the district of the Weaver on the whole, them is ro trade to important as the salt trade. Let tide flourish, and as a con- sequence the other indmitrial occupations cannot but more or less thrive. Let it flag and he depressed. and it casts a gloom over the district that all the other trades feel. last month we showed on an authority of the most reliable character thst the revival had commenced. It has gone on during the month: it still continues and we are sanguine enough to expect its continuance. The same good authority saya—, Ti,. resources of all makere have been taxed to the utmost, and in consequence of the abnormal drought of the early part of the year brine springs have not been able to supply all the calls made upon them, There ie, of course, abundant material, but it vent momentarily available. All these causes have contributed to increase prices materially. as a reference to the latest twice list will show. And that is hy no means representative of the highest figures which have born realised by some makers it only gives average quota- tions." It must be very gratifying to the salt proprietors to find a rise of Is. or Is. 61, per ton over prices which a month or two ago were below the proffiahle. And if these should. under the circomstances above nanied. continue to rise. we doubt not it will be atilt snore agreeable. The returns of the Custom House, Liverpool, for May. chow that more has not been shipped to the United States during any corresponding month, with the exception of 1179, for seven or eight years. And without any exreption this applies to our British North American provinces, to the West Indies, and to South America while to India more has gone than in any pre- vious year except 1875, when it wale little in excess of the current year. This etscressful traffic has no exception for Australia apparently. With Russia we only did more in the year 1876. when 19,381 tons stoml against 16,945 tons in 1880. With Russia we have done better than in 1875 and 1871), but considerable below 1874, 1876, 1877, and 1878. With regard to Holland we may do considerably better. CIITYTAL Ice—A new skating surface called "crernal ice" has been invented by fir. Calamariems, f tic.borough. Considering that after all ice is merely a crystalline sub- stance, and that there i. no lack of sehstances which are cryataline at ordinary temperature, Dr. Calantarients experimented with a variety of salts, and after a time suc- ceeded in making a mixture. conoistion mainly of carbonate and sulphate of soda, which, when laid as a Floor by his plan, can be skated on with ordinary ice skates. The re- .istance to the surface is just equal to that of ice. It looks like in,. and, indeed. .0..2 it hat toem sktted on and got "cut up" a little, the deception is quite astonishing. A small experimental floor has been laid on the skating rink at Prince's, and ha proved no succeesful that no doubt a large floor will be laid there, or at some other conveniett place, in the autumn. This door will obviously have great advantages, both over artificial ice tl.ads, nhich are very expensive indeed, and over Boors for roller skating. The surface can at any time be m..de smooth again by steaming with an apparatu. for the purpose, and the floor itself, when once lard. will heat for many years It is interesting to observe that the mixture of sal. uoed contains about 60 per cent, of water of crystallisation, so that, after all, the floor consiets chiefly of solidified water.—Noture. A letter was read from the Clerk to the Runcorn Corn. misaioner, as follows --I am directed by the Commis- sioners to draw your attention to au infectious case recently imported into Hunoorn from St. Helens. The facts as re- ported to the Commissioners are as tollows,—On Thurs- day, April 15tb, a child named Mary Ann Cotton, ag•-.1 54 years. living on the boat Ellen.of Manchester, registeled 2SO, was taken ill at St. Helens. She IRAs seen by a Doctor Martin, who gave her a bottle of medicine, and told the parents the child was suffering from s“rlet fever. The child was then brought in the boat to Sankey, and there died. On Sunday, the 113th April, the mother Rent to SE. Helen, and Dr. Martin gave hers certilieate that the child had died of scarlet fever. The dead body of the child was on the fol- lowing Tuesday, the 20th April, brought to Iluncom, and fortunately prompt measures were taken Icy the officers of this lioar.d, and the further progress of the inspection arrested. The Commissioners are of opinion that mses of this character are often the recant of spreading the infection, and deem it wise that the St. Helens Urban Autharity should be made acquainted with the facts of the above case."
